rankings.title: Delivery performance
rankings.intro: How infrastructure projects held to their budgets and their timetables. Every figure comes from the contract terms and costs recorded on each section, and a section appears only once the data supports the claim.
rankings.coverage: Measured on {lots} sections: {estimate} with an estimate-to-outturn comparison, {award} against the contract award, {completedSlip} delivered with a contract timetable, {ongoingSlip} still running.
rankings.coverageGap: The gaps are missing data, not clean records. A section without a recorded outturn cost or contracted duration cannot be measured, so it is left out rather than assumed on budget.
rankings.emptySlip: No section yet records both a contracted duration and an anchor date.
rankings.methodologyCosts: Costs carry the price year they were quoted in, and both sides of every comparison are restated into a common year before the percentage is taken, so an estimate made in 2013 is never measured directly against money spent in 2023. Costs recorded in different currencies are restated first and then converted to euro at that year's annual average exchange rate, in that order: converting first would use a rate from one year against prices from another.
rankings.methodologySchedule: Schedule slip uses the contract as the baseline rather than a press announcement, because that is the commitment the public paid for and the only baseline present for sections whose announced dates were never recorded. Negative values mean early.

table.sortHint: Sort by this column. Click again to reverse it, a third time to clear it.

performance.openedHelp: Every section that has opened, and how far past its contract date it ran. Sort by any column.
performance.costHelp: The best cost figure each section has: the outturn where one was published, otherwise the signed contract value, otherwise the pre-tender estimate. To rank them together each figure is restated into common prices and then converted to euro at that year's exchange rate. A section whose currency or price year falls outside those tables keeps its recorded cost but has no comparable figure, and sorts to the bottom.
performance.contractorHelp: Builders only, since a construction overrun belongs to whoever built the thing. Joint-venture work counts toward each partner, and name variants are resolved to one firm. Firms with a single section are left out.
performance.countryHelp: The same measures aggregated by country.
performance.emptyCost: No section yet records a cost figure of any kind.
performance.orderCost: Most expensive per kilometre first until you sort.
performance.orderGroup: Worst median slip first until you sort.

about.title: About
about.lead: A map of how countries actually build: what got finished, when it was promised, and what it cost.
about.dataBody: {projects} projects across {countries} countries, broken into {lots} sections, each with its own dates, cost, contractors and route. Sections are the unit that matters, because a motorway opens in pieces over decades and an average across the whole road hides that.
about.dataSources: Every figure comes from a public source that is cited on the project page. Where a number was never published, the field is left empty rather than filled with a guess, which is why some tables are shorter than you might expect. Routes are drawn from OpenStreetMap.
about.helpBody: The data is hand-curated, so gaps and mistakes are normal. Three ways to make it better:
about.helpReport: Spot something wrong or missing? Tell me what and where.
about.helpData: Add a country, a project or a missing cost figure. The data lives as plain JSON files with a cited source on every project.
about.helpSpread: Send it to someone who argues about infrastructure. Most of the interesting corrections come from people who already know the road.
about.builderBody: Simon Slanina. I started this because the answer to "how far behind is this motorway?" was scattered across press releases, tender notices and forum threads, and nobody had put it on one map.
